view: The garden became black from burning, like a dark night; ṣarīm can mean night. A cited poem uses it for a long dark night that dawn does not dispel, and one report singles out the exceptionally dark last night of a moonless month.
note: This contrasts with the readings in which the garden is white, bare, or like a harvested field.

view: The garden became white like dawn or like a dried, harvested crop; this reading takes ṣarīm as morning or dawn.
note: The disagreement with the night reading turns on whether the ruined garden appeared white or black.

view: The garden was like bare daylight: its trees and crops had vanished, leaving nothing in it.
note: This uses the day sense of ṣarīm, distinct from the dark night comparison.

view: The garden was like an orchard or field already harvested: its fruit was cut away or consumed, leaving none, though the trees may remain.
note: ʿAṭāʾ favors fruit cut off while trees remain and rejects explaining a fire as a harvested, cut-down orchard.

view: The garden's trees themselves were cut down or rendered like fruitless cut trees; one report says the whole orchard was severed from its roots and burned black like ash.
note: ʿAṭāʾ rejects the cut-down explanation because burning trees would not make the orchard look harvested; he favors loss of fruit while trees remain.

view: All the garden's goodness, especially its good fruit, was cut off, leaving nothing beneficial there.
note: This emphasizes the loss of good rather than a particular color or terrain.

view: The charred, fruitless garden resembled an isolated barren patch of sand, severed from a larger dune and unable to grow anything useful.
note: Al-Aṣmaʿī also gives ṣarāʾim for large separated sections of sand.

view: Al-Ṣarīm is said to be a known barren sandy tract or place in Yemen, called Ḍarwān in some reports; one locates Ḍarwān six miles from Ṣanʿāʾ.
note: This treats the simile as referring to a place, rather than to night, day, or a generic sand patch.

view: Ṣarīm is glossed as black ash in a reported dialectal usage, variously named Khudhaym, Khuzaima, Khuzaymī, Judhayma, or Khuzaʿa in the notes.
note: The dialect names vary across sources; the gloss is the shared point.

view: The burned garden was black like a black jar.
Both night and day are called ṣarīm because each is separated or cut off from the other; the word expresses severance.
note: This derivation supports either the night or the day reading.

view: Ṣarīm can specifically mean dawn or morning severed from night.
note: Al-Akhfash is repeatedly named for this explanation.

view: One derivation calls night ṣarīm because its darkness cuts off people's movement or sight; an objection says this cannot explain why day bears the same name.
note: Al-Qushayrī rejects the movement based derivation on the day usage.

view: Ṣarīm can be a passive-form adjective meaning maṣrūm, something cut off, like qatīl meaning maqtūl.
A derivation of ṣarīm for night takes it as an active form: darkness cuts off people's ability to move.
note: The source says this derivation does not explain the word's use for day.

view: Ṣarīm fundamentally denotes something wholly cut off or severed; its applications include cut fruit, a harvested field, a portion of night, and separated barren sand.
Aṣbaḥa means to enter the morning.
A heavenly visitor or divine command struck the garden at night while its owners slept; Arabic ṭāʾif ordinarily denotes a nighttime visitor, although daytime can be specified.
Fire destroyed the orchard overnight and consumed its fruit, leaving it scorched or blackened.
The sons at first thought they had lost their way, then recognized that their refusal to help the poor had brought the loss of the garden.
The loss of the garden's fruit may have been punishment or a trial that served as grace, since it brought the owners to repentance.

A Prophetic warning says disobedience can withhold provision already prepared for a person; the garden owners lost their crop because of sin. One version also names lost knowledge and missed night prayer.

The garden owners' worldly loss prefigures punishment for Quraysh; as with the brothers, repentance remains open to survivors. The parable answers people secure in their plans who call the Prophet possessed.

The disaster came wholly unexpectedly and devastated the orchard in an instant; attributing it to God highlights that sudden ruin, and ‘from your Lord’ reassures the Prophet amid Quraysh's apparent ease.
note: One description calls its reduction to nothing in a blink miraculous.

view: The heirs' sworn plan came true only to their harm and in an unforeseen way, without their carrying it out; their wish to take everything and deny charity ended in the orchard's complete ruin.
The pairing of aṣbaḥat, ‘it became morning,’ with ṣarīm understood as night creates antithesis.
The earlier yaṣrimunnahā and ṣarīm form paronomasia.
The word's several reported senses can all suit the ruined garden; one commentator favors retaining that range of meanings.
The following fāʾ in fa-tanādaw derives the owners' morning call to one another from their oath: they summon each other to carry out their plan.
Expanded accounts say the orchard belonged to a righteous man who left it to his people and town; they place it near Ṣanʿāʾ in Yemen, in Abyssinia, or among the People of Scripture.
One reported sense describes something severed from its destination, included among comparisons for the ruined garden.
In a dialogue with Nāfiʿ ibn al-Azraq, Ibn ʿAbbās says ṣarīm means gold and cites an anonymous poem using the word.
